title: Slain man was cop-kidnapper on run
article: The man who died in a shootout with Ontario police Sunday was being sought for violating his parole - after serving 10 years in prison for trying to kill a Montreal cop in 1991.

Daniel Lamer, 37, of Montreal, was a passenger in a Pontiac Sunfire when the car was pulled over on Highway 401 near Cornwall for a traffic violation. The lone Ontario Provincial Police officer requested backup after talking to the driver.

Shortly after two other police officers arrived, there was an exchange of gunfire that left Lamer dead. One of the OPP officers was slightly injured. Ontario's Special Investigations Unit, a civilian agency, is investigating.

But police representatives interviewed yesterday said they were upset to learn Lamer - who had a record for violent crime - was released on parole only 10 years after taking a Montreal Urban Community police officer hostage and nearly killing him.

"Unfortunately, we are not surprised," said David Griffin, of the Canadian Police Association. Coincidentally, the association of police unions was in Ottawa yesterday to lobby members of Parliament on several issues.
"We have made repeated complaints to the solicitor-general, the prime minister and members of Parliament that our corrections system is too lenient in dealing with violent offenders.
"It is inexcusable and unacceptable that these people are allowed to get out into the community, violate their parole and become fugitives."

On May 6, 1991, Lamer and another man held up a pharmacy on Sherbrooke St. for $68. The minor robbery developed into a hostage- taking after a Constable Richard Frohlich chased the pair into a tavern.

Lamer and his accomplice disarmed the constable, handcuffed him and tossed him into a car. Other police officers continued the pursuit but the constable was eventually dragged into a Bossuet St. duplex. The building was quickly surrounded by police but by that time a man living inside the building was taken hostage as well.

The ordeal ended 16 hours later when Frohlich managed to free himself, exchanged gunfire with Lamer and jumped out a window. Frohlich was wounded but survived and is still a member of the Montreal police.

On July 3, 1992, Lamer was sentenced to 22 years in prison after pleading guilty to attempted murder and several other charges in the hostage-taking. The lengthy sentence was in part attributed to the fact Lamer was on probation for a 1982 kidnapping at the time he took Frohlich hostage.

A National Parole Board spokesman said yesterday when Lamer returned to prison, his 22-year sentence was combined with time remaining from his previous term. So, Lamer was technically serving a 31-year sentence that started on June 21, 1982, when he was granted day parole from the minimum-security federal job-training centre in Laval on Nov. 3, 2000.
Early last year, Lamer failed to return to the job-training centre and, on March 29, 2001, a warrant for his arrest was issued.

In its written decision permitting day parole, the board noted Lamer was once addicted to cocaine and had a violent past. At the age of 17, he escaped from a prison van after grabbing a rifle and threatening the guards with it.

But the board members also considered that Lamer had successfully completed a series of escorted leaves and a work program at a mechanic's garage. The author of the report also noted a psychologist had determined Lamer had "completely separated himself from the criminal milieu" in the two years before he was granted day parole.
